MK: Diagnose accurately. Name the problem correctly as “burnout,” which may help the learner with identifying the severity of the problem.
SBP: Duty hours. Review weekly schedule vs. block schedules. Is the resident doing several stretches of nights? Is the learner moonlighting?
Work to get them time off.
Consider involving chief residents and/or residency leadership team in creating solutions that may aid this resident in their recovery from burnout - change in block schedule, time off, etc.
Use external support. If your hospital/GME office offers counseling sessions for residents, offer a referral to these. Offer wellness resources.
Targeted Mentorship. Match resident up with resident or faculty mentor who has overcome burnout for additional perspective.
The PD (and maybe the CCC) need to know if patterns of behavior are emerging for any one resident - they are uniquely positioned to have this perspective.
If it is a pattern of behavior, or is an egregious act, the resident may need some more dedicated coaching from the program.
If it is a personal issue (sick family member, etc), I encourage the learner to tell their PD, and offer to support them in any way they would like.
ICS: S: subjective (how did you feel?) – annoyed, disappointed, angry (“I felt disrespected when…”)
O: objective - what exactly did they do that made you feel that way? (focus on specific actions, behaviors, such as “I noticed you interrupted me 5 times during that session”)

A: assessment - what could be driving their undesired behavior? (“what was the reason for the many interruptions today?”) - you will not know the reason until you ask – many times the true reason for their behavior may surprise you!
Begin with “I’m on your side.” Emphasize motivation to help them improve. Often, this starts well before the conversation begins and extends to your entire relationship with the resident
Inquiry is telling the learner your concerns about it and asking for their thoughts.

“I noticed that you were very eager to share your thoughts during the conference session today.  I do appreciate your willingness to participate, however it seemed that you were interrupting multiple times in order to do this.  I am concerned that asking that many questions may not be well received by speakers.  Tell me about what you were thinking about today when you were asking questions.”
Be inquisitive. Either from a single advocacy inquiry statement or may require more “digging” to actually “get to the root of” why it is happening.
“I am interested to hear more about why you feel like this.” You may be (very!) surprised by the answer!
Empathize. Reassure learner that burnout is an occupational hazard and explore ways to recover.
Create alliance. Let the learner know that they have the support of the program and that other members of the department will step up in their time of need.
Discuss sleep hygiene and strategic sleeping.
What is the learner’s strategy for night shifts?  Are they getting enough sleep overall?
Are there unrecognized stressors that may be causing burnout or interfering with sleep?
What else is going on in the learner’s life?
PBLI: Addressing the behavior in the moment during a didactic session would be unlikely to be fruitful with this type of learner problem

P: plan – make a plan together for improvement going forward (use implementation intentions, described below). Essential to get their input and buy-in on this, as solutions won’t work if they are not on board.

Co-create a plan for future improvement. Have the learner first suggest ways they think they could improve their behavior. Modify the plan as needed.  Learners are more likely to be successful if they came up with the solution.
“Next time I want to interrupt, I will write down what I want to say and wait for an appropriate time to ask / say it”.
